title: 45-Day Identification Strategy
name: 45-Day Identification Strategy
metaTitle: 45-Day Identification Strategy in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: Pre-sourcing replacement candidates ahead of the 45-day clock, built around how fast port-adjacent industrial and infill product move in Los Angeles.

sections.html: The 45-day identification clock starts the day the relinquished property closes, and it does not pause for a slow search, a financing hiccup, or a candidate that falls through. In a market where port-adjacent industrial space near Vernon, Commerce, and the City of Industry can go under contract within days of listing, we do not treat 45 days as a search window at all; we treat it as a deadline to formalize a decision that groundwork should have already shaped.

sections.heading: Why Los Angeles Industrial Moves Faster Than the Clock Allows
sections.html:
Infill industrial scarcity around the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach means well-located buildings with clear ceiling heights and functional truck courts rarely sit on the market long enough for an exchanger to start a search from zero after their relinquished sale closes. We begin reviewing candidate industrial parcels, along with alternatives in multifamily, office, and retail depending on the exchanger's goals, weeks before a relinquished sale is even scheduled to close, so the identification list reflects properties already vetted rather than whatever happens to still be available on day 40.

This pre-sourcing work also lets us run a preliminary lender conversation on each candidate before it is ever named in writing, since a property that cannot realistically close within the 180-day exchange period is not worth the identification slot no matter how well it otherwise fits the exchanger's criteria.

sections.heading: Matching the Identification Rule to the Candidate List
sections.html:
• Three-property rule: name up to three candidates with no combined value ceiling
  • 200 percent rule: name any number of candidates as long as combined value stays under twice the sale price
  • 95 percent rule: name any number with no value cap, provided at least 95 percent of identified value is acquired
  • Choose the rule based on how many genuinely viable candidates exist, not how many are theoretically available
  • Confirm the rule selection with the qualified intermediary in writing before day 45

sections.heading: What a Written Identification Actually Requires
sections.html:
Identification must be delivered in writing, signed by the exchanger, and received by the qualified intermediary or another qualifying party before midnight on day 45. A property discussed verbally with a broker in Culver City or a seller near Torrance does not satisfy the requirement no matter how detailed the conversation, and each candidate has to be described unambiguously, typically through a legal description or street address, so there is no ambiguity later about what was actually named.

We confirm delivery separately from drafting the notice itself, since a completed identification letter sitting in an email draft folder does not count as delivered any more than an unsent fax would have decades ago. Nothing is treated as identified until confirmed receipt is in hand.

sections.heading: Building a Backup Into a Scarce Market
sections.html: A single-candidate identification leaves no room for a failed inspection, a financing delay, or a title issue discovered late, and that risk is higher in Los Angeles submarkets where competing buyers are actively bidding on the same limited inventory. We push exchangers toward naming at least one realistic alternative, whether a second industrial parcel, a multifamily property in a different rent-control jurisdiction, or a DST allocation held in reserve, because deep capital interest from both in-state and out-of-state buyers can move a primary candidate out from under an exchanger with very little warning.

sections.heading: Revising the List Before the Window Closes
sections.html:
An identification list can be amended any number of times before midnight on day 45, and we treat the first draft as a working document rather than a final answer, updating it as candidates fall out of contention or new inventory surfaces. Once the window closes, though, the list is locked regardless of what happens afterward in the market, which is why we push for the strongest possible list well before the deadline rather than waiting to see what late inventory appears.

We also keep a short list of secondary candidates in reserve even after the primary list is finalized, since a property that drops out of consideration for a reason unrelated to the exchange, a seller pulling out or a competing offer accepted elsewhere, can still be swapped in as long as the amended notice reaches the qualified intermediary before midnight on day 45.

faqs.q: When exactly does the 45-day identification period begin?
faqs.a: It begins on the day the relinquished property closes escrow, not on the day the exchange agreement is signed or the day the exchanger starts looking for replacement candidates.

faqs.q: Can a property be identified verbally to save time under deadline pressure?
faqs.a: No. Identification must be in writing, signed, and delivered to the qualified intermediary or another qualifying party before the deadline. A verbal mention to a broker or seller does not satisfy the requirement.

faqs.q: How does industrial scarcity near the ports affect identification strategy?
faqs.a: Because well-located industrial buildings move quickly, we begin sourcing candidates before the relinquished sale closes so the 45-day window is spent confirming a decision rather than starting a search from nothing.

faqs.q: Can the identification list be changed after it is submitted?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as any revision is delivered in writing before midnight on day 45. After that deadline, the list is fixed no matter how the market moves.

faqs.q: What is the consequence of missing the 45-day deadline entirely?
faqs.a: The exchange fails and the proceeds from the relinquished sale become taxable in that filing year, which is why we treat the deadline as fixed from the first day of the exchange.
